final_answer:
BOTTOM LINE. Yes, he has recourse, but it runs through two separate tracks, and the immigration-court track is the urgent one. (I could not retrieve the primary texts of several regulations directly, so several points below rest on secondary summaries of the regulations; see 'unresolved'.)

1. IMMIGRATION COURT (urgent). File a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order with the immigration court that issued it, under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii)) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). The 180-day 'exceptional circumstances' route under (C)(i) expired about January 28, 2026, so the motion must rest on lack of notice. Under (C)(ii) a motion based on not receiving notice under 240(b)(5)... 'in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2)' (NTA, or notice of hearing) may be filed at any time. Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), holds that the noncitizen loses if he received a valid paragraph (2) notice of hearing for the hearing missed, even where the NTA was defective. Here the husband's facts (NTA and, apparently, any hearing notices all mailed to an address he never provided) support a showing that he received neither a paragraph (1) nor a paragraph (2) notice. Key factual work: show the address used was never his address of record (I-130/I-485 listed the correct address; no AR-11/EOIR-33 obligation breached), that the court's notices went to that wrong address, and that he never received them. Note that notice by mail to the address he provided suffices even if not received, so the argument depends on the address being one he never provided; he must also show he did not receive actual notice from any source. Also be ready to address 240(b)(5)(A)-(B) (written notice by mail to the last address provided under 239(a)(1)(F), with the 'no address provided' exceptions), and whether any NTA lacking time/place (Pereira, Niz-Chavez) was cured by a later notice of hearing (Campos-Chaves).

Contents of the motion: the motion itself (a written motion with proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA; no special EOIR form is required for the motion), a sworn declaration from the husband (and wife, if helpful) describing the address history and non-receipt, evidence of the correct address (the I-130/I-485 filings, I-797 receipts showing the couple's address, lease/utility records, USCIS records), evidence that USCIS and the court used a different address, and a request for rescission and for an automatic stay of removal. Filing the motion within the in absentia lack-of-notice provision automatically stays removal pending decision (INA 240(b)(5)(C); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)). If represented, include Form EOIR-28; file via ECAS if available. Check for an EOIR-33 change-of-address. Also include copies of any relief application he intends to pursue (the court motion should state that he will renew his adjustment application before the judge; see below).

FEE. As of April 1, 2026: none. A motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) is exempt from the INA 286(m) fee and from the H.R. 1 (OBBBA) fee (8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii) as reported by secondary sources; the exemption is stated in the OBBBA fee rule/PM 25-36 as reported). By contrast, an ordinary motion to reopen before an IJ would cost $145 (286(m)) plus the OBBBA fee ($920 for FY2026, per secondary sources; $950 from Oct 1, 2026), and the IJ may waive fees for inability to pay. So the lack-of-notice motion should be filed with no fee; to protect himself, he can include a fee-waiver request alternatively only if the court treats it otherwise. If the court treats the motion as something other than a (C)(ii) motion (e.g., adds an alternative exceptional-circumstances argument, which would be untimely anyway), fees could be triggered; keep the motion framed under (C)(ii).

2. THE I-130 AND I-485 DENIALS (USCIS). The I-130 denial (Dec. 5, 2023) as abandonment for failure to respond to the RFE: normal remedies are a motion to reopen/reconsider with USCIS (Form I-290B, 8 CFR 103.5) or an appeal to the BIA (EOIR-29), each with a 30-day (33 if mailed) deadline that has long passed. USCIS may excuse a late motion to reopen where the delay was reasonable and beyond the petitioner's control (8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i)); non-delivery of the RFE and denial notices because USCIS used an address the couple never provided is a strong basis for that, and also supports arguing the I-130 denial was improper because no RFE was properly served. File the I-290B with USCIS promptly with evidence that the correct address was on the filings; the filing fee for I-290B applies (verify current USCIS fee). The I-485 denial cannot be appealed, but adjustment can be renewed before the immigration judge once the case is reopened (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii)); the IJ cannot adjudicate the I-130, so the I-130 must be revived/approved by USCIS (or on appeal). Adjustment eligibility itself: as an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen who was inspected and admitted, he is exempt from the 245(c) bars (overstay/unauthorized employment) under 245(a), but he must overcome the misrepresentation concern (B-2 entry on 12/1/2022 and marriage 19 days later, inside the State Department 90-day presumption of preconceived intent; INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i)), which is a significant merits risk, and the lack of a response to the RFE must be cured with bona fide marriage evidence. There is no stay of removal from a USCIS filing; the court motion is what protects him from removal. File the court motion first and quickly.

What must be filed with the court as of April 1, 2026: a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order based on lack of notice, with declaration, evidence, proof of service, a request for automatic stay, and (if represented) EOIR-28; no filing fee. Adjustment application renewal (Form I-485 with the court) and any fee questions come after reopening; EOIR itself charges no fee for the I-485, but USCIS biometrics and the OBBBA/other fees on other applications may apply (not verified).

authorities.title: Rescission of in absentia orders
authorities.proposition: In absentia order may be rescinded on motion within 180 days for exceptional circumstances, or at any time if no notice under paragraph (1) or (2); filing stays removal

authorities.title: Campos-Chaves v. Garland
authorities.proposition: Rescission for lack of notice unavailable if noncitizen received a valid paragraph (2) notice of hearing for the missed hearing, even if NTA defective; must show no notice under either paragraph (summary seen in search results only)

authorities.title: IJ motions to reopen in absentia; fees
authorities.proposition: No fee for in absentia motion to reopen under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii); IJ may waive fees for inability to pay (per search-result summaries; eCFR fetch blocked)

claims.text: A motion to reopen based on lack of notice may be filed at any time, so the 180-day window's expiry does not bar it.
Success depends on showing no valid NTA or notice of hearing under either paragraph; a proper later notice of hearing defeats rescission.
No court filing fee applies to a (C)(ii) lack-of-notice motion as of April 1, 2026; ordinary IJ motions carry 286(m) plus OBBBA fees, with possible waiver.
I-130 denial can be challenged by a late I-290B motion to USCIS if the delay was reasonable and beyond control; the I-485 can be renewed before the IJ after reopening.
